A little about me

Good design

I’m Ganen, a Product Designer with around seven years of experience shaping digital products, especially in banking and fintech. I enjoy untangling complex journeys and turning them into experiences that feel clear, considered, and dependable.

I work closely with product owners, product managers, engineers, and stakeholders in Agile teams—from understanding the problem and mapping flows to prototyping, refining UI, and supporting implementation.

My practice spans UX strategy, interaction design, design systems, usability thinking, and polished interface craft. I believe the best work balances customer needs, business goals, and the realities of building a product.

Case study · 01

Making digital onboarding easier to complete.

A redesign of the account-opening journey to reduce uncertainty, improve guidance and help more customers complete their first banking experience successfully.

RoleProduct Designer
TeamPO · PM · Engineers · Compliance
ScopeUX strategy · Flow · UI · Prototype
PlatformMobile banking

The challenge

New customers had to move through multiple steps before becoming active users. The experience needed to communicate requirements earlier and make progress feel more predictable.

1Too much information was presented at once.
2Users had limited visibility into what was required next.
3Validation and error states created avoidable friction.

The approach

I mapped the end-to-end journey, identified high-friction moments and worked with product and engineering to simplify the information architecture before moving into detailed UI.

→Clarified requirements before users entered each step.
→Reduced cognitive load through progressive disclosure.
→Designed clearer feedback for validation and recovery.
Outcome

Improved the account activation flow, contributing to higher first-time completion and a clearer path from sign-up to active banking.

Case study · 02

Making PayLater feel simple, not complicated.

Designing a clearer borrowing experience across discovery, application and repayment—while keeping important financial information visible.

RoleProduct Designer
ScopeUX · UI · Design system
FocusClarity · Trust · Conversion
PlatformDigital banking

Design principles

For a credit product, “easy to use” should not mean hiding important information. The interface makes cost, installment and repayment information understandable before commitment.

Key decisions

01Expose the important numbers at the moment they matter.
02Use consistent components to make the flow feel familiar.
03Separate promotional messaging from financial disclosures.
Design outcome

A more transparent PayLater journey that balances commercial messaging with customer confidence.

Turning “who owes what?” into a simple flow.

A UX study for splitting shared payments, designed around the social context behind the transaction—not just the transaction itself.

Problem framing

Splitting a bill is technically a payment task, but emotionally it is a coordination task. The experience needs to make amounts and responsibilities obvious without creating awkwardness between friends.

Solution direction

Introduce the shared expense first, make each participant’s amount explicit, then provide a lightweight request-and-confirmation loop.

Core insight

The best payment UX can disappear into the social moment it enables.

Case study · 04

Making everyday payments more flexible.

Expanding the payment experience with three simple ways to pay—Scan, Tap Beacon, and Show Barcode to the Cashier—so customers can choose an option that fits the situation.

RoleProduct Designer
TeamPO · PM · Engineers · Business
ScopeResearch · Flow · UI · Prototype
PlatformMobile banking · Payments

The challenge

Payment situations vary. Some customers can scan a QR code, others may prefer a quick tap, while some need to present a barcode at the cashier. A single interaction pattern may not suit every checkout context.

1Customers need to understand which payment method fits the situation.
2Each method requires clear instructions before the transaction begins.
3The experience should feel consistent without hiding method-specific steps.

Research & discovery

I framed the experience around the checkout context and the decisions customers need to make before paying. The key design question was how to make three distinct methods easy to recognise and use within one familiar payment journey.

→Mapped the steps and requirements for Scan, Tap Beacon, and Show Barcode to the Cashier.
→Identified where customers need guidance, readiness feedback, and clear next steps.
→Considered different merchant interactions while keeping the experience predictable.

Ideation & design approach

I explored a shared entry point that presents the three options in plain language, then guides customers through the steps specific to their chosen method.

→Use familiar labels and simple visual cues to help customers compare options.
→Keep each method focused on one primary action.
→Provide clear instructions for scanning, tapping, or presenting a barcode.

Key design decisions

01Scan: Make the QR-scanning action and camera step easy to find.
02Tap Beacon: Explain where and how to position the phone, with a clear ready state.
03Show Barcode to the Cashier: Give the barcode enough visual space and make it clear when to present it.
Design outcome

Three distinct payment methods, brought together in one clear experience that helps customers choose how to pay with confidence.
